Q29385419.summary: This large silver processional cross, its flaring arms ending in small finials, bears gilded medallions on the front: at the centre a bust of Christ, with the archangels above and below him and, to left and right, the Virgin Mary and John the Baptist interceding for humanity. Carried at the head of processions, it set Christ visibly at the heart of the Church's prayer, surrounded by the heavenly court.
facts: The Met notes that the front shows Christ with the archangels Michael and Gabriel above and below, and the Virgin and John the Forerunner to either side, the traditional intercessors.
An inscription on the back records it as the votive gift of a Bishop Leo; the back's central medallion shows Saint Thalelaios, a physician-martyr, with his medical case and lancet.
The cross measures about 59.5 × 43 cm and is dated c. 1000–1050.

cur:manuscripts-moralia-in-job-945-chris.summary: Christ stands frontally in a tall mandorla holding a book, set within a great red disc ringed with stars and flanked by two golden six-winged seraphim; red angels fill the upper corners, and below, the four evangelist symbols — man, lion, ox and eagle — stand on swirling wheels, each holding a book. A Latin inscription at the top describes the cherubim and seraphim crying out to one another.
facts: A colophon on fol. 500v records that the copying and illumination were completed on 11 April 945 by Florentius at the monastery of Valeránica.
The manuscript, with 502 folios of Gregory the Great's Commentary on Job, was later at Toledo Cathedral, where Arabic annotations were added, and entered the Biblioteca Nacional in 1869.
cur:manuscripts-moralia-in-job-945-chris.notes: Folio not stated on the Commons file; the Majestas is near the beginning of the manuscript.

wga:zearly/1/4mosaics/1rome/4cosma/cosma.summary: In a blue medallion on a gold ground, a white lamb lies on a jewelled throne before a tall golden cross; on the footstool below rests the scroll sealed with seven seals, and jewelled candlesticks with flames stand to either side. This is the Lamb of the Apocalypse, Christ slain and victorious, who alone is worthy to open the scroll of history. At the summit of the arch it greets the faithful before they see the great apse mosaic of Christ's return.
facts: The Lamb is flanked by seven candlesticks, four angels and the four creatures that are also the symbols of the evangelists.
The 24 elders who once offered their crowns to the Lamb were largely lost in the 17th-century rebuilding of the church; only some arms and wreaths survive.
Pope Felix IV turned the building into a church in 527, but the arch mosaics may be 6th century or later, perhaps 7th.

wga:zearly/1/4mosaics/1rome/4cosma/cosma.notes: WGA places this detail in the apse; it is on the triumphal arch. Dating of the arch relative to the apse (c. 530) is uncertain.
